body.text: Into every generation, a James Bond is born.
And with every new actor playing the British super spy, the franchise has had a reset.
A new Bond typically means a new look, a new tone and a chance to reinvent the 64-year-old film series for a new audience, and catch up with new trends.
It remains to be seen what the Robert Pattinson era will look like.
But here's how the anointing of a new Bond has worked out for the series previously, and how the changing face of 007 provides an insight into the history of action movies.
The Connery/Lazenby era
The first Bond film, Dr. No (1962), created a new template for spy films.
Its mix of humour, violence, sex and high-stakes action against a backdrop of world-shaping ramifications set the series apart.
Until then, spy films tended to focus on the cloak-and-dagger spycraft, and tried to keep both feet grounded in reality.
The big screen ambition of Dr. No was more akin to Alfred Hitchcock's groundbreaking North By Northwest (1959), where spectacle was preferable to plausible.

The Connery era of Bond quickly established the language of the films, such as the signature opening credits sequence, the dynamic score, the over-the-top villains with their over-the-top plans, the gadgets, the exotic settings, the highly questionable attitudes toward women, and the hero's mix of brawn, brains and babe magnetism.
Dr. No hit big at the box office, and Sean Connery was a big part of that — it's said that the phrase "men want to be him, women want to be with him" emerged because of him.
Within two years, a Bond parody was released (Carry On Spying), TV shows were aping the series (The Man From U.N.C.L.E.), and homages like Our Man Flint were in production.
Connery and co pumped out four films in four years, some of which are among the best and most successful movies of the series, notably Goldfinger (1964) and Thunderball (1965).
When Connery stepped aside after five films, George Lazenby took over for one ill-fated turn (On Her Majesty's Secret Service, 1969), which wasn't much of a reset, but more of a misfire.
Truckloads of money were thrown at Connery to ensure his return, and he re-teamed one last time with Goldfinger director Guy Hamilton for Diamonds Are Forever (1971).
But the magic was gone and something needed to change.
The Moore era
It is one of the best of the series, helped in no small part by Moore's ability to effortlessly slip into the role of Bond.
But as with Diamonds Are Forever, there are a few too many corny one-liners — a script tic that would come to be associated with Moore's stint as 007.
By Moore's second outing (1974's The Man With The Golden Gun), outside influences had started to creep into the series, which had previously defined itself as a trendsetter, not a follower.

The recent death of Bruce Lee and a rising interest in martial arts meant some cheesy Hollywood-style kung fu made an appearance, and this would not be the last example of Zeitgeist-chasing in the franchise.
In 1977, a little film called Star Wars became the biggest movie of all time, and everyone in Hollywood took notice, including the producers of the Bond franchise.
In response, 007 was launched into space in 1979 for Moonraker, the nadir of the franchise.

It was the biggest box office earner of the Moore era, but many critics were unkind, and opinions cooled even further as time went on. Moonraker was cited as the kind of film Mike Myers was thinking of when he created the Austin Powers series.
Moore and co would redeem themselves with For Your Eyes Only (1981), but after Moonraker, the franchise endured a steady decline at the box office.
By the time Moore bowed out with A View to a Kill in 1985, questions were being asked about where Bond fit in the world of 80s action.
The Dalton era

Despite just a two-year gap and rehiring director John Glen (who had done the past three Moore outings), Timothy Dalton's 007 debut in The Living Daylights (1987) felt like an abrupt change of direction.
Action movies had evolved since Moore's finale, A View to a Kill, went into production in mid-84.

The biggest films of 1984 had a darker edge to them that Bond lacked — Ghostbusters and Gremlins combined horror, sci-fi and comedy; Indiana Jones and the Temple of Doom featured people having their hearts ripped out; and Beverly Hills Cop starred a sweary Eddie Murphy investigating a bloody homicide.
Upon release, A View to a Kill was somewhat successful, but was far from the biggest action movie of 1985.
That honour went to the huge explosions and high body counts of Rambo: First Blood Part II, which made three times the amount of money in the US that A View to a Kill did.
In response, the Bond series took the hiring of Dalton as an opportunity to go darker and hit harder.
Dalton lasted just two films — The Living Daylights and 1989's Licence to Kill.
Both are less jokey and less cheesy without being humourless, and Dalton plays Bond with a barely contained rage to match a more violent tone.

The films were profitable, especially overseas, but American audiences shied away, preferring even more violent actioners such as Beverly Hills Cop II, Lethal Weapon, Predator and Robocop over The Living Daylights.

Dalton's second and final outing, Licence to Kill, is the lowest-grossing film of the franchise, and again it played well internationally, but fell well short in the US against other 1989 action blockbusters such as Batman, Lethal Weapon 2, Tango & Cash, Black Rain and about 30 other movies.
Many fans rejected the new approach, but there is a subset of Bond lovers that regard the short-lived Dalton era as the best of the franchise.
The Brosnan era
The series took its longest break between films — six years — before returning with Pierce Brosnan in the tuxedo, sipping on the shaken martinis.
A lot had changed in that time. Computers had taken over the world, the Cold War was over, and sexual harassment was finally acknowledged as a major problem.

Meanwhile, parents who had grown up with the Connery and Moore films were looking to take their kids to see a Bond film, meaning the series needed to ditch the darkness, especially if it wanted to sell a lot of Nintendo 64 games.

As a result, the producers used Brosnan to update Bond for generation X, even going so far as to get Dame Judi Dench's M to accurately call Bond a "sexist, misogynist dinosaur" and "a Cold War relic".
However there is still a sense of them having their cake and eating it too in the Brosnan era.

Denise Richards in short shorts as a nuclear physicist in The World Is Not Enough (1999) being a prime example, while Famke Janssen's Xenia Onatopp in GoldenEye (1995) is one step away from appearing in an Austin Powers film, but the treatment of women in the series has markedly improved.
But it is those aforementioned computers that had the most dramatic effect, with Jurassic Park up-ending filmmaking in 1993 by ushering in the age of computer-generated imagery (CGI).
The Bond series would embrace CGI in the Brosnan era, largely at the expense of the great stunts that had dominated the series.

GoldenEye still kept a toe in the stunt era with its riveting dam wall bungee jump in the opening, while Tomorrow Never Dies (1997) tipped its cap to the rising interest in stunt-heavy Hong Kong cinema by hiring the legendary Michelle Yeoh and featuring an insane motorbike chase through Bangkok.

But the CGI excesses are heavy in the finale of Brosnan's farewell Die Another Day (2002), and the film slowly disintegrates in a blizzard of laser beams, invisible cars, big wave surfing and ice palaces.
There would not be another Bond film for four years.
The Craig era
Someone arrived on the scene between the last Brosnan film in 2002 and the first Daniel Craig film in 2006, and changed everything.
His name was Jason Bourne.
Just as Bond had a literary spy pedigree via novelist Ian Fleming, Bourne was from the long-running Robert Ludlum novels.
But in the hands of Matt Damon and directors Doug Liman and Paul Greengrass, Bourne became something we had not seen in spy films before.

Combining improvised spycraft with the fast-cut editing and shaky cams of early millennial filmmaking, this was the anti-Bond — no gadgets, no CGI extravaganzas, no bikini-clad vixens, and no eccentric villains trying to take over the world.
For Craig's debut Casino Royale (2006), it was evident the Bond producers were watching Bourne and taking notes.
There were no gadgets, no obvious CGI extravaganzas, and no bikini-clad vixens, but the franchise did this without throwing the Bond out with bathwater.

Craig's 007 is still a debonair ladies' man who drinks and gambles, Mads Mikkelsen's blood-weeping baddie is a perfect mix of eccentric and terrifying, and the film features an incredible parkour sequence that's up there with the best stunt work in the series.

From Casino Royale onwards, the Craig era would attempt to keep one foot in reality and treat its Bond girls better, while simultaneously balancing its modernity and "wokeness" with obvious nods to the past.

Bit by bit, the gadgets, tricked-out cars and random shags returned, yet the series dug deeper as it went on, adding underlying themes, wider mythology-building and some ambitious visual ideas (check out the crazy long take that opens 2015's Spectre, or the silhouetted fight in 2012's Skyfall).
Craig bowed out in 2021 with No Time to Die, arguably the best send-off any Bond actor has ever had.
The future
In 1996, the US unleashed its answer to the James Bond series — Mission: Impossible.
But the initially sporadic output and limited cultural impact of the second and third films had minimal effect on the Bond franchise.
However the rebirth of the M:I series in 2011 brought some new spark, and arguably put Tom Cruise's Ethan Hunt on an equal footing with 007.

As Cruise hung onto airplanes, climbed the world's tallest building and drove motorbikes off mountains, he dragged the spy film back into the realm of real-world stunts, surpassing pretty much everything in the past few Craig outings.
Could this play a part in shaping the new Bond era?
The biggest competitor for box office bucks is superhero movies.
Where does a new Bond fit into a world where Black Widow and Captain America are running around with an endless array of god-like heroes with remarkable abilities?
The Craig era survived and thrived throughout this, but it had a running start.
The latest 007 will be trying to find out the hard way whether the world is ready for a millennial Bond.
